request.current_synthesis: The initial physical model makes acquisition and regulation competing consequential explanations. The arm starts fully extended at a singularity, actions are torque commands held for 20 ms, and success is determined by every one of 100 consecutive in-tolerance control observations. A fast policy may improve acquisition while causing overshoot; a policy that reaches the target may still fail the objective through residual motion or boundary crossings. The most credible first direction is to establish a baseline and measure mechanism-specific episode diagnostics rather than optimize a local distance or cumulative-in-tolerance proxy.

request.outcome: I1 resolved toward acquisition and trajectory selection as the dominant first baseline loss mechanism, with a secondary residual-motion regulation failure mode.
request.reason: T1 and M1 satisfy the closure condition. On the fixed 160-episode development panel, T1 achieved 151/160 successes (94.375%); among 9 failures, 6 never entered tolerance and 3 entered but were interrupted. Entry was common overall (96.25%), but failures concentrated in negative-angle strata, especially -135 to -90 degrees (80.8% success, 84.6% entry) and -180 to -135 degrees (84.0% success, 92.0% entry). Failed interruption events were high-speed exits with saturated actions, while median entry speed was 37.8 cm/s and the maximum was 286.3 cm/s. The evidence supports prioritizing acquisition/branch/trajectory robustness in the next intervention while retaining velocity-aware regulation as a secondary requirement.

request.description: Fine-tune T1 with a full-radius training distribution that oversamples negative target angles, minimum inverse-kinematic-branch progress shaping for elbow-trajectory selection, and a near-target joint-velocity penalty.
request.rationale: T1's six no-entry failures were concentrated in the negative-angle strata, where entry was slower and the -180 to -135 degree sector also had high entry speed. T1 was trained only on 14-20 cm targets, leaving the official inner-radius range underrepresented. This bounded transfer intervention exposes the complete official radius range, gives twice the training exposure to negative angles, explicitly rewards progress toward either valid elbow branch, and preserves uninterrupted-hold regulation pressure through a near-target velocity penalty. Comparing the resulting candidate with T1 on shared development seeds will test whether negative-angle acquisition and trajectory robustness improve without increasing high-speed hold interruptions.

request.description: Evaluate the two strongest T2 checkpoints and T1 on the shared 160-episode development panel, with paired diagnostics for acquisition, negative-angle strata, entry velocity, uninterrupted holds, and interruption events.
request.rationale: T2 training-window success peaks at 0.97 for checkpoints 65536 and 75776, while the final checkpoint declines to 0.89, so training reward does not identify a reliable endpoint. Measuring both peak candidates against T1 on identical episode seeds will determine whether the intervention improves the limiting negative-angle acquisition and trajectory outcomes and whether the near-target velocity shaping preserves uninterrupted regulation. The paired comparison is the required evidence for selecting a credible I2 candidate or redirecting the route.

request.outcome: I2 resolved as a qualified acquisition improvement that does not yet solve the coupled regulation problem. T2 improved shared-panel success from 151/160 (94.375%) to 153/160 (95.625%) and reduced no-entry failures from 6 to 4. The limiting -135 to -90 degree stratum improved from 21/26 successes (80.77%) and 22/26 entries (84.62%) to 23/26 successes and entries (88.46%), while the -180 to -135 degree stratum improved entry from 23/25 (92.0%) to 24/25 (96.0%) without improving success. Both T2 checkpoints retained three hold-interrupted episodes; entry speed increased from T1 median 37.76 cm/s to 65.51 cm/s for checkpoint 65536 and 71.98 cm/s for checkpoint 75776. T2 checkpoint 65536 is the stronger provisional candidate because it has lower entry speed than checkpoint 75776 at equal success, but neither is goal-ready.
request.reason: M2 satisfies I2's closure condition by providing shared-seed outcome, negative-angle acquisition and trajectory, entry-velocity, hold, and interruption comparisons. The intervention supports the acquisition/trajectory hypothesis, but the velocity-aware regulation guard did not preserve low-velocity arrival: T2's median and mean entry speeds rose materially, and hold interruptions remained at three episodes. The evidence therefore warrants a route change rather than treating T2 as a solution: retain the full-radius and negative-angle acquisition gains, but make convergence and saturated-action avoidance the primary next intervention.

request.description: Fine-tune the strongest T2 checkpoint with velocity-first convergence and regulation shaping: increase the near-target joint-velocity penalty and extend its activation band, penalize saturated actions near the target, and forfeit accumulated hold capital on any hold exit while preserving T2's full-radius and negative-angle training recipe.
request.rationale: T2:checkpoint-65536 retained the acquisition gain at 153/160 successes but entered at a median 65.51 cm/s and still produced three hold interruptions, all associated with high exit speed and saturated action. The existing velocity penalty is active only within 3 cm and is too small to compete with hold-progress reward, while hold exits currently forfeit no accumulated hold capital. This bounded transfer intervention tests the physical prediction that earlier velocity shedding and avoidance of saturated near-target corrections can convert T2's entries into uninterrupted holds without changing its demonstrated acquisition distribution or branch-progress shaping. The shared-seed measurement after training must compare overall success, negative-angle acquisition, entry velocity, saturation behavior, and hold interruptions against T1 and both T2 references.
